Ask HN: Why people keep posting AI-generated projects around the Internet?

Programming-related subreddits and other media platforms are current flooded by the waterfall of AI-generated projects. A typical post contains a problem description and the link to GitHub repo created just recently with sustainable amount of generated code in it. With the invite to review it, and to give a community feedback.

The quality of the projects vary, but very often these are codebases generated in a few days solely by the AI-agentic systems with little to no human review and prior history of development and recognition.

I'm asking this question not out of critiques. I genuinely don't understand motivation and the roots of this phenomena.

Asking for the professional code review seems to be pointless for the publisher. Many of them didn't have prior experience in the programming language in which the code has been generated. Furthermore, the code is seemingly not interested for the publisher either. It does not look to me as a good start for community-driven (F)OSS project anyway.

Another motivation that I can imaging is seeking for public recognition. But considering the amount of postings, I think it's highly unlikely in the current situation even for the genuinely high-effort works.

I can also assume that some are seeking for the self promotion by faking professional skills with AI assistance. That might be true for some, but the majority don't hide the fact that the presented code has been generated. It's unlikely the main motivation too.

So, I completely lost in understanding on what's going on, and what steams this never-stopping process. At a first glance the author doesn't gain anything in return, and I don't understand what they are seeking for.
label: Qualitative

text:
Show HN: Risphai – picks the AI model, tools and prompt for each request

I noticed that a lot of non-technical people don’t use AI to its full extent. Like they use the wrong model for the task, the wrong reasoning effort, or vague prompts. That gap between "what the AI can do" and "what people actually get" is what I wanted to fix.

So I spent the last two years in my spare time building a consumer AI product that tries to fix this issue.

This is how it works:
When it receives the request, an LLM decides the task type (chat, reasoning, coding, writing) and the tool calls that are needed (web search, image generation, video generation, audio generation). Then it routes it to a suitable model and applies a prompt based on the task type. If it's a media generation task, it rewrites the prompt into a detailed one using prompt formulas (the prompt formulas for specific styles are mentioned in the system prompt). The LLM that is used for answering the request can also use a map, generate a mermaid diagram, generate a quiz or flashcards, generate files, etc.

A limitation right now is that routing adds latency, but I'm currently experimenting with decision-models like Jev, PPLX Decider, etc. and might use decision-models to route to the right LLM and give the tool calls like web search and media generation to the answering LLM.

It launched this week, so it's still early and I will keep improving it and adding new things.

Also sign-up/in is required to prevent abuse.

I’d really like honest feedback: what’s confusing, what’s missing, etc.

text: Why the Creators of AI Do Not Understand Their Own Creations Just citations. Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic, 2025): "People outside the field are often surprised and alarmed to learn that we do not understand how our own AI creations work. This lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology." MIT Technology Review: "Despite all the stunning success, nobody really knows how — or why — it works." Yoshua Bengio (Turing Award laureate, 2024): "If we continue as before, we are driving against the wall. Or at least we are driving into a fog, without knowing whether there is a wall." Mathematician Roman Vershynin (UC Irvine), in a recent interview — "We advanced to the wall and hit it." So why did AI research hit the wall? The answer is not hard to find, and most people in the field know it, even if they prefer not to say it loudly. The point is that all training data used by AI is secondary, while the primary source is the human being. Every text, every image, every pattern a neural network absorbs — all of it was created by humans. A neural network does not discover the laws of the world; it only finds regularities in what has already been created by human intelligence. So if we want to understand how AI forms knowledge, we must first understand how humans form knowledge. But this pretty obvious idea was never materialized because of the historical failure of all attempts to build a working, mathematically correct model of knowledge. The story started in the 19th century and continued until the end of the 20th. Tens of theories of information, hundreds of books, thousands of articles in dozens of journals — and nothing practically working came out of it. This however does not mean no adequate theory exists. It is there since the late 2000s, but it is still completely unknown to the scientific community. This occurs for a purely ideological reason because this theory builds its formalizations on concepts borrowed from mainstream programming languages and so completely ignores mathematics. For the major journals devoted to AI and information theory that is a taboo. I spent years trying to publish it. The answer was always the same: "Add the mathematical justification, and then we will take a look." When I contacted established researchers directly, the answer was either silence or: "Yes, you have an original idea, but we are not interested." I stopped trying fifteen years ago. My hope is that now the theory might have a chance, because it addresses exactly the problems that the current conceptual apparatus cannot solve. The Theory of Meaningful Information (TMI) expands the conceptual framework of the most expressive programming language, which is C++, by adding capabilities for creating standard narrative (non-executable) texts that constitute the primary form of any human language. In TMI, information is defined as the value of a variable used in some algorithm. This works for a bit in a computer, a state of a neuron, a pressed button, a written letter. It applies to a bacterium, a program, a neural network, and a human. The theory introduces Information Capable Entities (ICE) and traces their evolution from the simplest biological ICE — a cell — to complex technical devices and the human being, who is modeled as an object controlled by a biocomputer (the brain). It offers a complete algorithm of human knowledge formation, from the simplest perceptions to the most complex concepts. It contains the theory of intelligence, covering both natural and artificial intelligence, and the theory of a universal representation language. A short description of TMI and a link to the complete work: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23403895 Boris Sunik, independent researcher

text: Show HN: Animated step-by-step hints for any cryptic crossword clue Cryptic crosswords are fun AND hard, and I've recently been introducing easier ones to my 11y/o daughter. It made me realise that when you're stuck, all you can do is hope you somehow come up with the way to crack it, or look at the answer and have all the satisfaction of figuring it out yourself removed! I also realised that when I was explaining to her how clues worked, I would scribble all manner of letters, arrows doodles to make sense of how the words of the clue could be mangled and eventually produce the answer. So I made a thing that would replicate the pencil and paper solving process, and create stepped visual animations that would enable you to get just enough info to make solving it within your reach, so you could feel like you did enough of the working out to get that "Aha!" feeling, without just getting straight to the answer. You can paste in any cryptic clue with its length, e.g. "Around Los Angeles, coatless dudes make AI model, say (6)", and the animation shows you how to solve it, one step at a time. It's split into 3 or 4 sections, which most cryptic clues fit into: 1. Which end of the clue is the definition 2. What type of clue is it (there are several conventions in the cryptic world, a clue can be 1 of these, or a combination of several) 3. What are the pieces used to build the answer 4. How do the pieces fit together to create the answer You can stop as soon as you have enough info to get you back to solving it yourself. It was easy to get a smart AI to solve the clue - but it was trickier to get it to be reliable and correct. LLMs can be very good at writing a confident, plausible breakdown for a completely wrong answer! So I needed to use a multi-pass approach: 1. A small, fast model checks that the input looks like a cryptic clue. 2. A more capable model solves it and writes a step-by-step breakdown. 3. Another independent model solves it "blind", without seeing the first attempt or its answer. 4. A "judge" then checks that the two solvers agree on the answer and method, and that the letters in the breakdown actually add up to the answer. If that fails, it tells you it’s unsure instead of bluffing, and if it’s only fairly sure that the answer and "how to" is the correct one, it says so. The breakdown of how the clue is solved is then drawn as an animation, step by step, with letters and meanings scribbled and manipulated the way you'd do if you solving it yourself on paper. Depending on the complexity, a clue usually takes between about 10 to 30 seconds to be solved. There's a cache, so clues that have already been solved once can be returned without going through the AI process again. It can still get things wrong, especially on loose clues or ones with some flexibility in how they can be interpreted, but generally it performs pretty well. Your first clue solve is free, and an account gets you two more. There are paid plans to cover the AI costs involved for multiple solves as there is a cost to it. There's also some good resources for learning cryptic crosswords basics - and a library of clues with hints to practice with. You can also write and share your own cryptic clues - along with the hint animation generated for them "https://crypticinkling.co.uk/create" rel="nofollow">https://crypticinkling.co.uk/create I’d love feedback from any cryptic crossword ninjas or beginners alike. PS here's the breakdown for the clue at the top of this post: "Around Los Angeles, coatless dudes make AI model, say (6)" - how many hints do you need to crack it? Tell HN: Anthropic found 36 bugs (6 CVEs) in Pion, OpenAI missed them

We added Pion DTLS to Anthropic's OSS scanner last week (https://github.com/anthropics/oss-scanner/pull/93), and today we woke up to a report with 36 bugs, including 6 security vulnerabilities: 2 critical, 3 high, and 1 moderate. Four of them affect WebRTC.

Some of these vulnerabilities have been sitting in the codebase for over 4 years, surviving years of testing and security scans. It's funny that our inboxes are constantly spammed with AI-generated security reports from people using Codex and Claude, most of which flag pointless issues. Yet somehow, none of them caught these.

The funniest part? Anthropic also found 3 bugs that OpenAI's internal code review missed. I had asked OpenAI to review a new DTLS API since they use Pion and had a use case for it in SPED. Their review didn't flag any bugs. Anthropic found an authentication issue, a deadlock, and a TLS KeyUpdate bug (Maybe their model ignored this one because it's not a WebRTC issue). Luckily, the API hasn't been released yet. The fixes: https://github.com/pion/dtls/pull/1236

Here are the security advisories for the CVEs Anthropic found (all of them are pre-chatgpt!):

Critical: DTLS handshake signature confusion allows peer impersonation - https://github.com/pion/dtls/security/advisories/GHSA-7c2r-jhm9-43vf

Show HN: Gondwana, a code-first C#/.NET game engine with WebGL

Gondwana is a 2D/2.5D game engine for C#/.NET 8 that I’ve been building over the past 16 months, using SkiaSharp for rendering. I've spent my career creating web and distributed apps and that has influenced the engine's development, so it will feel very familiar to anyone with a similar background. The engine is deliberately code-first in its implementation but still includes visual authoring tools and a custom CLI.

I started creating Gondwana to host my own RTS and SNES-style games, to offload the game ideas percolating in my brain. I wanted to focus more on creating gameplay systems and was less concerned with 3D graphics. The predictability and transparency of the old Win32/GDI era were the ideal for what I was shooting for, but I also wanted something faster and more portable than GDI32. To that end, I am not trying to emulate the bigger engines.

Spot! became my primary dogfooding project that I’ve since pushed up to itch.io. Getting a game to that point really helped burn away the cruft that accumulates from trying to create something like this. I was able to get Spot! to render at a consistent 120 fps on my dev machine. I experienced the absolute ecstasy of getting WebGL to cooperate with the engine cycle. And I discovered that even if Gondwana is code-first, you don’t want to hand-code platformer levels, so I added Gondwana Studio to the repository. Studio uses the same file formats that are understood by the core engine. Asset handling was beefed up, UI widgets were added for things like game HUD elements and engine diagnostics, and I fleshed out the CI/release pipeline to keep it organized.

As it stands currently, Gondwana supports GPU-backed OpenGL rendering with WinForms and Avalonia hosts, and a dedicated WebGL path with Blazor. Recently a good bit of effort has been put into optimizing the rendering hot-path, reducing contention between simulation and presentation, and into making the visual tooling easy to use by people other than just me. I even was able to get itch.io deployment down to a single command in the custom CLI.

The engine is still actively evolving feature-wise, but the core rendering is pretty solid right now. I expect Gondwana will remain 2D/2.5D with parallax support, so I am not trying to supplant Unity, Godot, et al. Also worth noting, Gondwana intentionally does not have an explicit ECS framework built in, although one could absolutely work well with the engine if desired.

The project is MIT licensed, the source is hosted on GitHub, the packages are on NuGet, and Spot! is playable in the browser at itch.io. I will include several links in the first comment under this. I’d love to see what other hobbyists or indie game devs think of the project. Feedback on usability, as well as praise and/or criticism of the architecture would be awesome.

Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast

Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

text:
Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug

I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.

The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.

Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.

To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.

Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism:
Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":

1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.

2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.

3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.

The Support Wall:
I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.

As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.

If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.

Pura vida!

Show HN: Muse Jailbreak – Let Muse use your own Chrome

Hi HN. I built a small macOS menu bar app that lets the Muse agent use the Chrome browser on your own Mac.

I built it because I kept hitting the same wall. I'd ask Muse to do something on the web and it would come back holding a login page. I'm already signed in to a thousand places in my own Chrome; I don't want to hand every one of those logins over to an agent, or sign in all over again inside some cloud browser. So I built a bridge that lets Muse use the browser I already have: my Chrome, my sessions, signed in as me.

How it works: the app launches a dedicated Chrome profile on your Mac and exposes it over CDP. You turn it on, it shows a one-time code, you give that code to Muse, and Muse connects through a tunnel (Cloudflare Quick Tunnel by default, or a self-hosted sish fallback if you prefer your own infrastructure). The browser never leaves your machine: cookies, sessions and logins stay on your computer. The tunnel only carries the agent's control traffic, and it is end-to-end encrypted (AES-256-GCM). Muse sees screenshots and sends back clicks and keystrokes; where a page needs a genuine mouse event it can also click at the OS level via the Accessibility API.

It is native Swift with no third-party dependencies, and everything is open source (app, protocol, tunnel client) so you can audit exactly what it does before running it.

Honest caveats: this gives an AI real control of a browser where you are logged in. That is the point, and also the risk. Use the dedicated profile, don't leave it running unattended, and only connect agents you trust. macOS only for now.

I built it for my own use and would genuinely like feedback on the security model: what is missing, and what would make you comfortable (or uncomfortable) running something like this?

Show HN: Sufuku – Sudoku, but Numbers Repeat

Sudoku is short for "the digits must be single". I wondered if inverting this would work: "the digits must be repeated". And so, by swapping "doku" for "fuku", Sufuku was born.

In short, instead of using numbers 1-9 for a 9x9 board, you use 2 twice, 3 three times, and 4 four times (for a total of 9).

It plays differently from sudoku than I expected. I assumed it would be simpler, since you have fewer digits. But once I settled on irregular region shapes, I discovered that it can also be quite difficult. In sudoku you eliminate a number by placing it; in sufuku a number is only eliminated once all its copies are placed. So you count lines instead of mostly scanning the board.

As I want the game to be approachable, the daily boards are mostly 6x6 or 7x7 for now. Larger boards are more interesting because 6x6 has only one set of numbers: [1, 2, 3]. But for 9x9 you can go with [2, 3, 4], [1, 3, 5], or [1, 2, 6] (I skip pairs like [2, 7] because I consider them boring). 10x10 is the first one that offers a set of four numbers: [1, 2, 3, 4].

Of course it turns out the idea has been around for some time: 2-3-4 Sudoku (Uwe Wiedemann) and Sudoku Ripeto (Miguel Palomo). I'm curious what you make of it as a daily game.

Today's Friday, so the board is on the harder side. You can play easier boards in this week's archive.

Show HN: Trustmux – Async tmux from your phone, now in Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency. That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone. I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS. Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile? - SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile. - Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants. Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit. Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome. Quick start: 
  trustmux enable
  trustmux start
  trustmux pair   # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed
Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store. Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project. Show HN: Kitaphone – Call mobile phones and landlines directly from the browser

Hi HN Folks,

I have been building Kitaphone a web app that lets you call regular mobile and landline numbers directly from your browser. The idea is simple, there are still plenty of situations where apps like WhatsApp, facetime and other internet calling apps aren't an option. For example, when you are abroad and need to call your bank, an airline, or a government office or your son/daughter's school.

I wanted to make those calls possible without requiring users to install another app or buy a sim card or even commit to a monthly subscription. I built Kitaphone using Next.js and Twilio, One of the more interesting challenges has been making browser based calling reliable, especially when it comes to dealing with microphone permissions, sending keypad inputs to automated phone systems, and preventing abuse of free calling credits.

The product is live and supports international calls to regular phone numbers, users currently need an account to make calls partly because each call has a real telecom cost. I am still improving it and learning from the people using it by receiving feedback.

Fun fact: "kita" means our in Bahasa Malaysia, since I am based in this beautiful country and their people are so warm and welcoming I was truly inspired by this place and decided to name it our phone.

Interested to know or receive feedback from HN folks who worked with WebRTC or VoiP in the past.

text: Show HN: Endo – A Higher-Order Harness Endo is a Higher-Order Harness (HOH). From the easiest concept to understand to the more complex ones, Endo gives you: * A single, simple UI to use any agent provider with your existing subscriptions, and hot-swap agents right in the middle of a session. * An orchestration layer, which I call HOH, allowing arbitrary composition of agents to achieve any workflow. A fun case I tried was asking Fable and Astra to mock a presidential debate. * An agent protocol that abstracts any agent. The key insight here is that every LLM is an agent—instead of treating the LLM as just one node inside an external ReAct loop. Endo was a concept formed while I was building OpenChart ("https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart" rel="nofollow">https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart). To power trading workflows, I needed to support scenarios where strict determinism is required, while still keeping the flexibility of an agent's inference-time decision-making capability. A new form factor was needed between rigid n8n-style workflows and open-ended ReAct loop agents. Thus the creation of Endo. Endo is short for Endomorphism, a term rooted in category theory and functional programming. An endomorphism is a function that transforms an object into another object of the same type. Similarly, Endo itself is built purely on functional programming principles, relying heavily on Effect ("https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect" rel="nofollow">https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect). ..And if you have patience to speak technical jargons, Endo is: * An agent orchestration layer—Higher-Order Harness (HOH)—where an entire agent is treated the same as a single LLM call, enabling arbitrary composition of extremely complex workflows. * A way to abstract any harness into a standardized protocol, where raw models and agents behave the exact same way, in a KV-cache-friendly manner. * A workflow engine that enables arbitrary composition of agents with a single workflow language. It's completely open source, and if you think this idea is cool, let's build together. Just for the fun of it.

text: Show HN: RDST – A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning. Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: - manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables - see which queries are slowest - figure out what indexes are missing - figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes - painstakingly implement a fix In the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you. Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions. We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change. How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST. RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix. We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years. RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries. Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here. "https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy" rel="nofollow">https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy We really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free. Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time. We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands. Let us know what you think!

text:
Show HN: Relay – A Mac app that adds /relay command to Claude, Codex and Cursor

Simply put, Relay is just a copy-paster between Claude, Codex and Cursor. It adds a /relay command to those GUIs that just sends the chat history since last over to the other side.

I’ve been working on this small Mac app called Kanary that offers essential features. While building it, I found myself stupidly repeating the process of being a messenger between Claude and Codex.

Then I thought, why not build a feature that helps my development process? What if Kanary could be a meta-app that bridges between harnesses? That’s when I hit on the idea of a meta harness. A wrapper that works IN the GUI apps that we already use, not a new app.

It’s still just a copy-paster, but it has changed how I work tremendously. So far it’s a painkiller for me, not a vitamin. I’d love to hear what you think of this simple tool that does this one simple thing.

75 free relays per week. Copy is always free.

Show HN: RickCV, a modern resume builder where you can drag&drop your old CV

*You can drag and drop your old resume, and with a little luck, most of the data will be imported, which can at least serve as a good starting point.

I initially built RickCV a few months ago as a simple template for an HTML resume and have continued to refine it over time. I and many people in my personal circle enjoy using it and have had success with it.
It’s a relatively playful approach that might not be to everyone’s taste. It currently supports the following formats:

- German cover letter following the layout rules of DIN 5008

- English cover letter, in A4 or US Letter.

I hope you find it as useful as we do.

text: A misbehaving test MCP server for stress-testing your MCP client We needed an MCP server that misbehaves on our command to test our own MCP gateway at work, but could only find well-behaved MCPs. That’s why we built a misbehaving MCP server ourselves and now share it on here, might be helpful for others building MCP gateways. It’s similar to the MCP Inspector, but lets you test your client not your server. We called it MCP Test Kitchen and it’s a (also hosted) MCP server that lets you: * Connect any client that takes a URL and an Authorization header (Cursor, Claude Desktop or your own). It answers both 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 clients and logs which protocol revision each request declared. * Pick one of 6 scenarios: HTTP transport errors, JSON-RPC error responses, tool results flagged isError, elicitation, multi round-trip requests (MRTR) via a C# SDK v2 scenario, and a baseline with a configurable delay. JSON-RPC and tool errors can be set to fail on a specific call, so the first call succeeds and the second fails. Resources and prompts are always on, each with a deliberately broken variant. If you want other scenarios, let us know. * Watch every request in a live log with timing, method, caller, status and protocol version. * Clone a TypeScript reference client, pinned to the latest spec, with full source. You can run it yourself, it’s open source. If you’d rather test it live, we also hosted it, but you need to login (Google or GitHub, needed for the token) and can get started immediately. We’d appreciate feedback, that’s why we're posting. In the live tool, there is a box that emails us directly.
